title: Why this matters for the lab
objective: Connect sensitization to chemogenetic silencing of visceral afferents.

steps.title: If the afferents drive it, silence them
steps.body: If sensitized visceral afferents drive hypersensitivity, then quieting them should reduce it. The field already shows **chemogenetic silencing** of nociceptors can lower inflammation-driven hypersensitivity — evidence that these neurons are *necessary* for it, not just correlated.

steps.setup: In an inflamed gut, you silence the relevant sensory afferents with an [[hM4Di]] [[DREADD]] and give the actuator.
steps.prompt: What do you predict for hypersensitivity?
options: It should decrease if those afferents drive it
It should increase, since silencing removes an inhibitory brake
It should be unchanged, because hM4Di acts only on the cell body
Only conduction velocity in those afferents should change
steps.reveal: Silencing the afferents tests causation: if they carry the hypersensitivity, quieting them reduces it. This is the chemogenetic logic (C5) applied to a disease model — and the template for probing other organs.

variants.prompt: Chemogenetically silencing sensitized gut afferents should…
options: Reduce hypersensitivity if they drive it
Increase it, by removing an inhibitory brake
Change only the conduction speed, nothing else
variants.explanation: Silencing tests whether those afferents are causal for the hypersensitivity.

steps.prompt: Why does silencing (loss-of-function) strengthen a causal claim here?
options: If removing their activity removes the symptom, they're likely necessary
Silencing on its own shows that the neurons are sufficient for the symptom
If silencing changed nothing, that would prove the neurons play no role
Silencing a whole population rules out every other pathway at once
steps.explanation: Loss-of-function tests *necessity*: no activity, no symptom → the neurons are required. (Showing *sufficiency* would need gain-of-function — driving them to evoke the symptom.)

variants.setup: Silencing the afferents abolishes the hypersensitivity.
options: They are sufficient on their own
variants.reveal: Loss-of-function shows necessity; sufficiency needs a separate gain-of-function test.

sources.note: Reviews chemogenetic silencing of nociceptors reducing inflammatory hypersensitivity.

reviewNotes: Chemogenetic silencing of afferents; necessity vs sufficiency; project tie-in.
